podcast.title: First Hit with "Money (That's What I Want)" (1960)
podcast.body: "Money (That's What I Want)," written by Janie Bradford and Berry Gordy, became the first hit for the newly formed Motown Records in 1960 after Barrett Strong recorded it for the Tamla label. "It would go on to become the first hit for the new Motown Records in 1960."

podcast.body: Following the UK chart success of "The Tears of a Clown," Motown's home office decided to release the single in America in October 1970, leading to its number one hit status by December. "That's when Motown's home office decided to try the single in America."

podcast.title: Motown's British Division Strategy (1970)
podcast.body: Motown's British division strategically chose "The Tears of a Clown" for release in the UK in July 1970 to celebrate The Miracles' success and fill a market gap while Smokey Robinson was on hiatus, recognizing its "throwback Motown classic" sound. "Motown's British division chose the track for release in the UK to celebrate the miracle's success and fill a market gap while Smokey was on hiatus."

podcast.title: "Hit Factory" Reputation
podcast.body: Motown was known for being a "hit factory," implying a focus on producing popular records rather than a "think tank" for artistic experimentation, though this changed for Stevie Wonder's "Songs in the Key of Life." "very gory the founder of motown which was known for being a hit factory not a think tank said of stevy wonder he took his life experience and put it all into songs in the key of life and it worked."

podcast.title: "Motown Sound" and "Sound of Young America"
podcast.body: "Please Mr. Postman" was the first number one hit from Motown that distinctly featured "the Motown Sound" and simultaneously established the label as "the sound of Young America," solidifying its musical identity. "So today we're going to look at the first number one to come out of Motown, a record that definitely did have the Motown Sound, and which established the label as the sound of Young America."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: "The Sound of Young America"
podcast.body: Motown's output, particularly its major hits from groups like Martha and the Van Dellers, is epitomized by the phrase "The Sound of Young America." Even decades later, these records continue to capture the essence of this sound. "When you hear them now, even almost 60 years later, you're still hearing the sound they were in at the birth of. The sound of Young America."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Artist Lack of Creative Control
podcast.body: Typically, Motown artists had "no say in what songs they recorded," reflecting a strict hierarchical control over their creative output. This policy meant groups like The Supremes often had to record material they disliked. "Normally, Motown artists have no say in what songs they recorded."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Barry Gordy's Praise for Stevie Wonder
podcast.body: Motown Founder Barry Gordy lauded Stevie Wonder's 1976 album, *Songs in the Key of Life*, remarking that Stevie successfully took his life experiences and "put them all into this album and it worked." "Motown Founder Barry Gordy said that Stevie took his life experiences and they put them all into this album and it worked."

podcast.title: Barry Gordy's Rejection of "One Bad Apple"
podcast.body: Motown's Berry Gordy famously turned down the song "One Bad Apple" for his superstar family band, The Jackson 5. The song was then remade by The Osmond Brothers into an "uncanny Jackson 5 facsimile" and became a number one hit, inadvertently affirming The Jackson 5's imperial status by showing their influence on other acts. "A song Motown's Barry Gordy turned down for his superstar family band that was then remade by the Osmond Brothers into an uncanny Jackson 5 facsimile."

podcast.title: Beginning of Domination
podcast.body: Following the release of "Come and Get These Memories" by Martha and the Van Dellers, Motown began a period of chart domination in America that lasted the rest of the decade, largely attributed to the songwriting and production of Holland, Dozier and Holland. This era is considered Motown's "true golden age." "it began a domination of the American charts that would last the rest of the decade, a domination caused in large part by the team of Holland, Dozier and Holland."

podcast.title: Beverly Hills Residence of Barry Gordy and Diana Ross
podcast.body: Motown president Barry Gordy and Diana Ross, whom he described as the love of his life, resided in Beverly Hills. The Jackson 5 also moved into their residence after leaving Gary, Indiana. "This is where the Jackson's were living with Motown president Barry Gordy and the woman he described as the love of his life Diana Ross."

podcast.title: Bobby Jean Hall's Extensive Contributions
podcast.body: Bobby Jean Hall was a prolific percussionist whose work is featured on a vast number of Motown records. Her contributions were integral to recordings by seminal artists like The Temptations, Diana Ross and The Supremes, and Smokey Robinson and The Miracles. "Bobby Jean Hall is an all-around percussionist who can be heard on a ton of Motown records, including recordings by the temptations, Diana Rosses and The Spremes, and Smokey Robinson in The Miracles."

podcast.body: Bruno Mars signed with Motown Records for a year in his early career, although this deal did not ultimately lead to any recorded releases. However, it proved significant as it facilitated his introduction to Philip Lawrence, with whom he would later form a highly successful songwriting partnership. "Bruno even signed with Motown records for a year, but no recordings resulted from that deal."

podcast.title: Criticism for Lack of Political Content
podcast.body: Motown faced criticism from African Americans for its perceived reluctance to be more politically outspoken in its music. This was largely due to Berry Gordy's cautious approach, as he remained hesitant about overtly political messaging in his releases until the early 1970s. "Like James Brown Motown was also criticized by African Americans for not being a little more political but Barry Gordy was always afraid of that at least up until the early 1970s."

podcast.title: Crossover Goal vs. Black Power Ethos
podcast.body: Historically, Motown's primary goal was to achieve crossover success with a white audience, as this guaranteed radio play and increased record sales. However, this objective became antithetical to the core principles of the Black Power movement, which prioritized black self-determination and cultural pride over seeking approval or acceptance from white audiences. "Yes, that was the goal in the past especially for Motown because crossing over to a white audience meant radio play and record sales but it would be counter to the whole goal of the black power movement to care if white people liked the soul music that was being produced."

podcast.title: Demo Destruction Policy
podcast.body: Motown pressed about 250 demo copies of Frank Wilson's "Do I Love You Indeed I Do?" in 1965, but these were largely destroyed because Motown head Berry Gordy did not believe the demo was any good, resulting in only 2 to 5 copies surviving. "About 250 copies of the demo were pressed up because neither Wilson nor Motown had buried gordy, but that the demo was any good. Those 250 records were destroyed, except maybe between two and at most five copies."

podcast.title: Discovery of Important Black Artists
podcast.body: Motown was renowned for discovering and launching the careers of numerous important black artists, including Lionel Richie and Tina Turner. "descubrió la nera de la niña del Richie, descubrió la tina, tarné, descubrió a todos los artistas negros importantes."

podcast.title: Evolving Slogan: "Create, Sell, and Collect"
podcast.body: Barry Gordy's original Motown slogan, "create, make, and sell," was changed to "create, sell, and collect." This revision reflected his realization that simply selling records was insufficient if the label wasn't getting paid by distributors, highlighting the crucial business aspect of the music industry. "He changed that slogan to create, sell, and collect."

podcast.title: Exclusion of First #1 Artists from Anniversaries
podcast.body: Despite The Marvelettes being the first group to score a number one hit for Motown, none of its original members were invited to participate in any of the label's 25th, 40th, 50th, or 60th-anniversary celebrations or TV specials. "None of the members of the first group to hit number one on the label were invited to be part of any of them."

podcast.title: Financial Crisis and "Please Mr. Postman"
podcast.body: Following the million-selling "Shop Around," Motown's subsequent releases performed poorly, leading to a severe financial crisis. Distributors were not paying for records, pushing the label close to bankruptcy; "Please Mr. Postman" was the critical hit that saved Motown by ensuring they got paid for past successes. "And please Mr. Postman was the record that saved Motown. I've talked before about how a hit record could put a small label out of business."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 93: "Please Mr. Postman" by the Marvelettes

podcast.title: Financial Structure for Creative Workers
podcast.body: Motown's financial structure imposed royalty charges on creative workers, including producers and songwriters, for studio time. This system meant that if a recorded track was not released, the creative team would incur financial losses, influencing decisions like passing on rejected songs to other artists. "Motown caused problems for its creative workers was that they would be charged against royalties for studio time."

podcast.title: First Big Hit with "Money"
podcast.body: Motown (under the Tamla family of labels) achieved its first significant success with Barrett Strong's "Money," though this record did not yet embody the distinct "Motown Sound" that would define the label. "When we left at the Tamler Motown family of labels, a couple of months back, they'd finally had their first big hit with Barrett Strong's Money"

podcast.title: Hitsville U.S.A. as a Creative Hub
podcast.body: Hitsville U.S.A., Motown's studio, was a bustling environment where aspiring artists, including The Primettes, would "hang around" and often find opportunities to contribute minor session work, such as handclaps and backing vocals, fostering a unique pathway into the label. "They took to hanging around Hitzville, acting like they belonged there, and they soon found themselves during minor bits of work on sessions, handclaps and backing vocals and so on."

podcast.body: Motown Records was one of the most important record labels, known for producing all significant records in black music, including genres like R&B, funk, 1960s disco, and romantic music, particularly between the 1960s and 1970s. "la visina de las discurráficas más importantes y la música que he dicho todos los discos importantes para que antes de los años 60 y 70 sobre todo en lo que fue la música negra, el ratal blar, el funky, la música disco de los años 60 incluso la música más romántica."

podcast.title: Learned Distribution from Sadie DuPouy
podcast.body: Berry Gordy, the founder of Motown Records, was taught how to make distribution deals for artists on his label by Sadie DuPouy. This crucial knowledge contributed significantly to Motown's eventual success and its ability to effectively get its music to audiences. "And it was she who taught Barry Gordy about how to make distribution deals for artists on his own Motown Records."

srcs.episode: Driven By Her: Unsung Heroines

podcast.title: Move to Los Angeles
podcast.body: In the early 1970s, Motown Records relocated its operations from Detroit to Los Angeles. This move prompted some artists, like Martha Reeves, to decide not to make the transition with the label, leading to the dissolution of groups like Martha and the Van Dellers. "When Motown moved from Detroit to LA in the early 70s, Martha was one of those who decided not to make the move with the label"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 111: "Heat Wave" by Martha and the Vandellas

podcast.title: Multitracking System Innovation
podcast.body: Mickey Stevenson instituted a new multitracking system at Motown, moving away from recording all musicians, lead singers, and backing vocalists simultaneously. This allowed backing tracks to be recorded separately by The Funk Brothers, with vocals overdubbed later, improving efficiency and flexibility. It also enabled reusing backing tracks for different artists (e.g., The Miracles' hits for Marvelettes covers) and replacing singers if unsuitable. "Now, backing tracks would be recorded by the Funt Brothers in the studio, whenever a writer produced her had something for them to record, and then the singer would come in later and overdubbed their vocals when it was convenient to do that."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 111: "Heat Wave" by Martha and the Vandellas

podcast.title: Ownership of Group Names
podcast.body: Motown, rather than the artists, owned the names of its groups, a practice that allowed the label to sell off names like "The Marvelettes" after groups disbanded. This meant original members had to tour under modified names. "Motein, rather than the women, had owned the group name and had sold it off."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 93: "Please Mr. Postman" by the Marvelettes

podcast.title: Policy for Hit Follow-Ups
podcast.body: Motown adopted a strict policy: after an artist had a hit, the same producers and songwriters were assigned to create new material that sounded similar to the original hit. Artists were only permitted to diverge from this formula once their current hit-making strategy ceased to be successful. "This would be the policy from this point on with Motown. If someone had a hit, the same producers and songwriters would be a sign to come up with something that sounded like the hit, and the artist would only go in a different direction once they stopped having hits with their original formula."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 93: "Please Mr. Postman" by the Marvelettes

podcast.title: Shift from Formulaic Sound
podcast.body: By 1971, Motown began to move away from its established and highly popular formula, particularly one that had found widespread acceptance among white audiences. This evolution allowed for a "very different funky or sound," as exemplified by songs like The Undisputed Truth's "Smiling Faces Sometimes." "It's 1971 and Motown is finally starting to get out of that formula that they had that was so popular in particular with white people that's a very different funky or sound for Motown."

podcast.title: Slump Period (Pre-"Where Did Our Love Go")
podcast.body: Prior to the success of "Where Did Our Love Go," Motown Records was experiencing a slump, characterized by disappointing follow-ups from several major stars and the departure of one of its biggest artists, Mary Wells, to another label. "Mo Tan was in a bit of a slump at that point. Several of the label's big stars had had disappointing follow-ups to their hits, and they'd just lost Mary Wells one of their biggest stars to another label."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Stevie Wonder's Contract and Artistic Freedom
podcast.body: Stevie Wonder's departure from his contract with Motown Records freed him to explore new musical directions, specifically with synthesizers. This allowed him to collaborate with Malcolm Cecil and Robert Margouleff on the TONTO synthesizer to create the music he envisioned, leading to some of his most acclaimed work. "Stevie was out of his old contract with Motown Records and wanted a tutorial and synthesizers so he could finally start recording the music that he heard in his head."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Unsung Heroes of Music: Part 1

podcast.title: Union Rule Circumvention
podcast.body: The Musician's Union had a rule requiring a vocalist to be present if musicians were cutting a vocal track. Motown, like other labels, often broke this rule. A surprise union inspection during a Mary Wells session led Mickey Stevenson to have his secretary, Martha Reeves, sing the lead to avoid penalties, ultimately leading to Martha taking over the song. "Motown, like most labels, were perfectly happy to break the union rules on occasion, but there was always the possibility of a surprise union inspection"

podcast.title: We Are The World Inception Point
podcast.body: The initial idea to create and record the song "We Are The World," and to gather all the participating artists, was conceived at the Motown house. "la idea de grabar el disco, la idea de la canción, la idea de contra todos los artistas, se gestó en la casa de la mota."
